reason: The sources across three distinct websites provide corroborated astrometric and photometric evidence confirming the first isolated stellar-mass black hole.
story: For decades, every stellar-mass black hole ever detected was trapped in a binary dance, revealed only because it was actively devouring a companion star. Astronomers knew millions of solitary black holes should be silently prowling the Milky Way, completely invisible and untraceable. That changed with OGLE-2011-BLG-0462. When an invisible phantom drifted in front of a background star in the Galactic bulge, its immense gravity warped spacetime, acting as a gravitational microlens that magnified and deflected the background star's light. Ground-based surveys and the Hubble Space Telescope tracked the precise deflection over six years, eventually extending the baseline to eleven years across sixteen telescopes. The data proved the invisible object weighs over seven times the mass of the Sun yet radiates zero detectable light. Hurled through space by a supernova kick at over fifty kilometers per second, it is the first confirmed rogue black hole wandering entirely alone through our galaxy.
angle: Astronomers caught the first confirmed rogue black hole wandering completely alone and invisible through the Milky Way, weighing over seven times the Sun's mass.

claims.claim: OGLE-2011-BLG-0462 is an isolated stellar-mass black hole drifting through interstellar space.
The object is also identified as MOA-2011-BLG-191.
OGLE-2011-BLG-0462 is the first unambiguously confirmed isolated stellar-mass black hole.
The black hole was detected via gravitational microlensing as it passed in front of a background star.
The microlensing event occurred in the direction of the Galactic bulge.
The black hole's gravity caused relativistic astrometric deflections of the background star's light.
The Hubble Space Telescope was used to measure the astrometric deflection over multiple observational epochs.
It took six years of initial observations to confirm the existence and nature of the black hole.
The latest analysis determined the mass of the black hole lens to be 7.15 solar masses (plus or minus 0.83).
The black hole emits no detectable light, verifying its nature as an isolated dark remnant.
The black hole lies at a distance of approximately 1.52 kiloparsecs (plus or minus 0.15 kpc).
The black hole is traveling with a space velocity of approximately 51.1 kilometers per second relative to nearby stars.
The observational baseline for astrometry was extended from 6 years across 8 epochs to 11 years across 11 epochs.
Photometric modeling incorporated observational data collected from 16 different ground-based telescopes.
The lensed source star is situated just 0.4 arcseconds away from a much brighter neighboring star.
Astronomers conducted systematic searches for binary companions to the black hole and found no evidence for any.

disputed: Distance to the black hole: Wikipedia cites 1,720 parsecs (5,610 light-years), whereas the updated Sahu et al. 2025 papers derive 1.52 +/- 0.15 kiloparsecs (and earlier 1.58 kpc). Scripts should attribute the distance as approximately 5,000 light-years or cite the latest 1.52 kiloparsecs measurement.

Object mass: Lam et al. initially reported a lower mass range of 1.6 to 4.4 solar masses suggesting a possible neutron star, but subsequent re-analyses by Mroz et al., Lam and Lu, and Sahu et al. converged on roughly 7.15 to 7.88 solar masses, confirming a black hole. Scripts should state the consensus mass is around 7 solar masses.
